title: Glory in kindness (Jeremiah 9:22–23)
hook: let no one glory in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God of kindness and justice
carry: here, in kitchens and courts and streets

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah asked why there was no healing when the balm was right there in Gilead. Your line was he stays, and he hurts with them. Who did you bring a little to? Today, a few verses on, the same prophet talks about bragging. Day eight hundred one.
screen: `HE STAYS, AND HE HURTS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Scroll any feed for a minute and the boasts sort themselves into three piles. Look how smart I am: the degree, the hot take, the clever reply. Look how strong I am: the workout, the win, the promotion. Look how much I have: the car, the kitchen, the trip. The piles have changed their clothes over the centuries, but not their shape. Jeremiah names all three in one breath, and then tells you the one thing worth boasting about. It isn't any of them.
screen: `SMART, STRONG, RICH.` → `THE BOASTS HAVEN'T CHANGED.` → `ONE THING WORTH BOASTING ABOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches." Wisdom, might, riches: the three piles. Notice that the verse doesn't say they're bad. Being wise is good; being strong is useful; money can do a lot. It only says they're not what to glory in. Then the turn. "But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." Three Hebrew words: chesed, kindness; mishpat, justice; tzedakah, righteousness. Three boasts out; three of God's ways in. And look at the strange shape of the boast. It isn't I am kind. It's I know a God who does kindness. To know God, in this verse, is to understand what God does and delights in. And where? In the earth. Not only in heaven, but here, in kitchens and courts and streets. In the last chapter of his Guide for the Perplexed, the philosopher Maimonides turns to this very verse. His reading, in brief: knowing God leads somewhere practical, to acting with kindness, justice and righteousness yourself. So the verse that starts as a ban on bragging ends, in Maimonides' reading, as a job description: the one boast it allows is knowing what God delights in, and that knowing is meant to show in the hands.
screen: `NOT WISDOM, NOT MIGHT, NOT RICHES.` · then, large: `KINDNESS, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · then: `IN THE EARTH.` · `MAIMONIDES' LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: boast only of a kindness. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days. Find one moment of kindness you saw, or were given, or managed to give. Someone held a door, covered a shift, said the right word. Hold it for a moment, and let it be the thing that matters about your week. If it was someone else's kindness, plan to tell someone about it today, out loud, with their name. Jeremiah's verse allows one boast, knowing the God who delights in kindness; telling someone else's kindness is a small way of pointing to it. If you pray, you can hold his words: for in these things I delight. The bell holds the time.
Chesed. Hebrew for kindness: not in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God who does kindness, justice and righteousness in the earth. Today's word.
Your line: here, in kitchens and courts and streets. Today, if you catch yourself about to show off, tell a story about someone's kindness instead. Day eight hundred one.

howItsDone: These verses close the haftarah read in synagogue on the morning of Tisha b'Av, so the day of mourning's reading from the Prophets ends on kindness, justice and righteousness.

notes: KJV 9:23–24 = JPS 9:22–23 (the index's numbering). Quoted from the KJV because I was not certain of the exact JPS 1917 wording.
Maimonides, Guide III:54, closes the Guide on Jeremiah 9:22–23; the summary of his reading (knowledge of God leading to imitation of these ways) is a paraphrase. Please check.
howItsDone: the Tisha b'Av morning haftarah (Jeremiah 8:13–9:23) ends on these verses. Please confirm.
The hook's three 'piles' is the writer's framing of the verse's three boasts.

Editor: fixed a garbled line ('three ways of God's in'); softened 'Maimonides closes his Guide with this verse' to his last chapter turning to it (screen, match and trapdoor too); corrected the practice, which misstated the verse's one allowed boast.

Audit: the teach's last lines told the listener what to boast of ('if you want to boast, boast that you know what God delights in'); reframed as Maimonides' reading. Smoothed 'three words come back in Hebrew'.
